## India's ₹72,000 Crore Seafood Export Industry Runs on One Invisible Ingredient: Temperature

Behind every shrimp that travels from Andhra Pradesh to America lies an
unbroken chain — invisible, relentless, and absolutely non-negotiable.

### ₹73,890 Cr

India's seafood export earnings, FY 2025–26

### 19.7 LMT

Metric tonnes exported — an all-time high

### 66%

Share of frozen shrimp in total export value

When people think about India's seafood exports, they picture fishing
boats, processing plants, and international trade. Very few think about
**temperature.** Yet temperature may be the single most critical factor
determining whether a shipment reaches international shelves — or gets
rejected before it ever reaches consumers.India's seafood exports
recently crossed ₹72,000 crore, making the country one of the world's
leading suppliers.1 Frozen shrimp alone contributes more than two-thirds
of export earnings. But behind every export container lies an invisible
system working 24 hours a day. That system is the cold chain.*A shrimp
harvested in Andhra Pradesh and eaten in New York never once had the
luxury of warming up.*

## The product that cannot afford a mistake

Unlike manufactured goods, seafood starts losing quality the moment it
is harvested. Every minute matters. A shrimp from an aquaculture farm in
Andhra Pradesh may travel thousands of kilometres before reaching a
restaurant in New York, Tokyo, Dubai, or Amsterdam.During that journey,
it must remain within strict temperature ranges — not for hours, not for
days, but for the entire supply chain. Because seafood buyers aren't
simply purchasing shrimp or fish. They're purchasing consistency,
freshness, and food safety.

## India's export success story

India exported nearly 19.7 lakh metric tonnes of seafood in FY 2025–26,
generating approximately ₹73,890 crore in export earnings.2 Frozen
shrimp remained the dominant product, contributing more than ₹49,000
crore and accounting for over 66% of total export earnings.WHAT THE
NUMBERS MEANIndia isn't just exporting seafood — it's exporting
temperature- sensitive products to some of the world's most demanding
regulatory markets. Every shipment depends on uninterrupted cold chain
infrastructure from harvest to destination port.

## The journey nobody sees

Most people only see the finished export. They don't see the five
temperature-controlled stages that every shipment must survive without
exception.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| 1 | **Harvest** | Fresh seafood must be cooled immediately. Any delay begins the deterioration process — there is no recovering lost time. |
| 2 | **Processing** | Cleaning, grading, packing, and export preparation — temperature control is critical throughout every handling step. |
| 3 | **Blast freezing** | Rapid freezing locks in freshness and minimises cellular damage. This stage largely determines the final export quality. |
| 4 | **Cold storage** | Products await transportation while maintaining strict temperature conditions — sometimes for days, sometimes for weeks. |
| 5 | **Reefer container transport** | Specialised refrigerated containers carry cargo from facility to port to international destination — the final, longest leg of the chain. |

## Why reefer containers matter more than ships

Many assume the vessel is the most important part of international
logistics. For seafood exporters, that's not true. The most critical
piece of equipment is often the reefer container — a mobile cold storage
facility whose sole job is to maintain product temperature despite:

- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Tropical heat
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Long transit times
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Port delays
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Customs inspections
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Weather disruptions
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Power fluctuations

Without reefer technology, large-scale seafood exports simply wouldn't
be possible at the scale India operates today.

## When temperature becomes money

A shipment doesn't have to spoil completely to create losses. Even minor
temperature deviations in highly regulated export markets can result in:

- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Reduced shelf life on arrival
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Quality claims from buyers
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Export rejections at port
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Reduced market price realisation
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Long-term brand reputation damage

In highly regulated export markets, consistency often matters as much as
product quality itself.

## The new challenges facing exporters

India's seafood industry is growing rapidly, but it is also facing
increasing pressure. Recent international trade disruptions — including
tariff uncertainties and container movement challenges — have
demonstrated how vulnerable seafood supply chains can become when
logistics are disrupted.Exporters must now navigate rising compliance
requirements, shipping delays, global trade uncertainty, and
ever-tightening quality control expectations from international buyers.
This makes cold chain resilience not just valuable, but essential.*The
future of seafood exports isn't built only on what we catch. It's built
on how well we preserve it.them.*

## The future of seafood exports is infrastructure

India already knows how to produce world-class seafood. The next
challenge is preserving that quality across longer and more complex
global supply chains. That's where infrastructure investment will define
the next phase of growth.

- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Blast freezers that lock in freshness at the source
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Cold storage facilities with uninterrupted power backup
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Reefer containers engineered for long-haul reliability
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Real-time temperature monitoring across the supply chain
- ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
  Temperature-controlled logistics from farm to export port

Because seafood exports don't compete on price alone. They compete on
quality, consistency, and the reliability of the cold chain behind every
shipment.

## Final thought

A seafood shipment may travel across oceans. Its success, however,
depends on a single number that must never change: temperature.Behind
every exported shrimp, every sealed container, and every record-breaking
trade figure is a cold chain system working silently — and invisibly —
in the background. As India's seafood exports continue breaking records,
one truth holds firm across every market, every shipment, and every
freezer hold:The strongest cold chains are not the coldest ones. They
are the most consistent ones. [Go Back](/blog)
